reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in SCN2A encoding the Nav1.2 voltage-gated sodium channel expressed in excitatory neurons

The functional effect largely dictates phenotype and treatment: early-onset (neonatal-infantile) seizures usually reflect gain-of-function, while later-onset seizures, autism or intellectual disability often reflect loss-of-function
Early-onset gain-of-function cases frequently respond well to sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure medications
In contrast, later-onset loss-of-function cases may be worsened by sodium-channel blockers, so age at onset guides drug choice
The spectrum ranges from self-limited familial neonatal-infantile seizures to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
Autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability without epilepsy are recognised presentations, particularly with loss-of-function variants
Genetic testing with functional interpretation is central to management
reference.pathophysiology: SCN2A encephalopathy is caused by variants in SCN2A encoding the Nav1.2 sodium channel, which mediates action-potential initiation and propagation in excitatory neurons, especially early in development. Gain-of-function variants increase sodium current and neuronal excitability, producing early-onset seizures that respond to sodium-channel blockade. Loss-of-function variants reduce excitatory signalling and impair network development, more often causing later-onset seizures, autism and intellectual disability, and such cases may deteriorate with sodium-channel-blocking agents. This mechanistic dichotomy makes age at onset a practical proxy for the underlying channel effect.
additionalDifferentials: Autism spectrum disorder with or without epilepsy
Other early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: SCN2A testing or an epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing with functional interpretation
EEG appropriate to age and seizure type
Brain MRI to exclude structural pathology
redFlags: Refractory neonatal or infantile seizures with developmental arrest
Seizure aggravation after starting a sodium-channel-blocking agent in a later-onset case
Diagnostic uncertainty between gain- and loss-of-function phenotypes affecting drug choice
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable and correlates with variant type and age at onset, ranging from self-limited neonatal-infantile seizures with normal development to severe drug-resistant epilepsy with profound disability. Later-onset loss-of-function cases frequently have autism and intellectual disability regardless of seizure control.
pitfalls: Applying a single treatment strategy without regard to age at onset and channel effect
Using sodium-channel blockers in later-onset loss-of-function cases and worsening seizures
Overlooking SCN2A in autism or intellectual disability without prominent epilepsy
Interpreting a variant of uncertain significance without functional or phenotypic context
